newsitem.title: USA: US mutual fund dips hurt asset prices little-study.
newsitem.headline: US mutual fund dips hurt asset prices little-study.

text.p: The short-term effect of asset market returns on U.S. mutual funds has been "too weak" to sustain a downward spiral in stock and bond prices, according to a 10-year study reported in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's latest Economic Policy Review.
The study also found that bond fund flows were more sensitive to market returns than stock fund flows.

Examining the relationship between mutual fund flows and short-term market returns on a monthly basis from 1986 to 1996, the study found that, on average, mutual fund inflows have tended to accompany market upturns and outflows have tended to accompany downturns.
Despite investors' fears of a market crash, however, the short-term effect of market returns on mutual fund flows "typically has been too weak to sustain a spiral," the study said.

"During unusually severe market declines, stock and bond movements have prompted proportionately greater outflows than under normal conditions, but even at these times, the effect has not seemed strong enough to perpetuate a sharp fall in asset prices," it said.
The study revealed further that the funds with more conservative investment objectives also are the ones most vulnerable to outflows.
For example, bond fund flows, rather than stock fund flows, were more sensitive to market returns, and income funds were more subject to outflows than growth and global stock funds.

The researchers studied mutual fund flows during the past five severe market declines: the bond market in April 1987 and February 1994, the stock market in October 1987, the stock and high yield bond markets in October 1989, and the municipal bond market in November 1994.

Although market returns did in fact have stronger effects on mutual fund flows during these periods, the effects were still "not strong enough to sustain a downward spiral in asset prices," the study concluded.

Three stock fund groups -- growth, income and global equity -- and five bond fund groups -- government, corporate, municipal, Government National Mortgage Association and high yield -- were used for the study.
